title: The Russian MoD Said It Intercepted 323 Ukrainian Drones Overnight. The Same MoD Statement Lists 19 Russian Regions, the Sea of Azov, and the Black Sea as Affected. Razvozhayev Then Admitted Sevastopol Lost Power. The SBU Confirmed Four Hangars Hit at Saky and Two S-400 + Two Pantsir-S1 Systems Near Kerch
narrative:
On the night of 24-25 June 2026, the Russian Ministry of Defence claimed that Russian air defense systems 'allegedly intercepted and destroyed 323 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight.' The Russian MoD statement, published 25 June at 11:12 local time, listed 19 Russian regions affected by the overnight attack: Astrakhan, Belgorod, Bryansk, Voronezh, Volgograd, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Nizhny Novgorod, Oryol, Orenburg, Penza, Smolensk, Tula, the Moscow region, Krasnodar Krai, and occupied Crimea. Russia also claimed drones were destroyed over the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

In Russian-occupied Crimea, Moscow-installed Sevastopol governor Mikhail Razvozhayev said a Ukrainian air attack had 'knocked out power in its largest city' overnight. Razvozhayev's Telegram message stated: 'The enemy is again striking vilely, trying to deprive us of our usual living conditions and sow panic. We will not be intimidated by the lack of light. We have gone through more than that, and we will survive now.' He warned that some areas would be left without power until Wednesday evening and that a 'special regime' had been put in place at energy facilities as damage was assessed.

The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and Ukraine's Special Operations Forces said on 24 June that drone operators from the 'Alpha' Special Operations Center carried out strikes on infrastructure in the Kerch Strait area, as well as at the Saky and Hvardiiske military airfields. The SBU said the operation damaged four aircraft storage hangars at the Saky military airfield. Near Kerch, Ukrainian forces also struck two components of a Russian S-400 air defense system and two Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.

Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, said on Wednesday that drones had targeted 48 operational and planned military sites in Crimea and that the main power substation of Sevastopol had been hit. Monitoring channels also reported strikes against energy infrastructure on the peninsula. Half of Crimea was without electricity after the overnight strikes. Gas stations in occupied Crimea were instructed to fully suspend fuel sales to civilians from 21 June.

analysis:
Three findings structure this story, and each one names a specific evidentiary layer that the prior Russian-strike coverage did not contain.

First, the 323-drone Russian MoD claim is contradicted by the MoD's own geography. The Russian MoD's '323 drones intercepted overnight' figure implies near-total denial — but the same MoD statement lists 19 Russian regions affected, occupied Crimea, the Sea of Azov, and the Black Sea. A 'near-total interception' that hits 19 regions, the Sea of Azov, and the Black Sea is operationally incoherent. The MoD's own geography contradicts its own count. The 19-region list reads as a tour of Russian federal subjects — not as a list of nearly-missed targets. The 'near-total interception' framing cannot be reconciled with strikes of this geographic dispersion.

Second, Razvozhayev's 'lack of light' admission is the first on-record acknowledgement from a Russian-installed official that a Ukrainian strike had knocked out power in Sevastopol, the largest city in Russian-occupied Crimea. The phrase 'we will not be intimidated by the lack of light' implicitly concedes that the power outage is real and lasting — 'until Wednesday evening' per the same Telegram post. Razvozhayev's 'special regime' formulation is the same language Russian-occupation authorities used in previous major strikes on Crimean energy infrastructure. It indicates the strike was not a near-miss at the substation but a confirmed hit that activated emergency protocols. The 21 June civilian gas-sales suspension (three days before the 24 June overnight strike) is the cumulative layer: Russian-occupation authorities have now been forced into sustained fuel-sales suspension since 21 June — the first documented instance of this during the war.

Third, the SBU confirmed high-value strategic-asset damage that is incompatible with the 323-interception claim. The SBU said the operation damaged 'four aircraft storage hangars at the Saky military airfield' and 'two components of a Russian S-400 air defense system and two Pantsir-S1 air defense systems' near Kerch. These are high-value Russian strategic assets, not civilian infrastructure. The 323-interception claim is incompatible with strikes of this precision. Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, publicly claimed 48 operational and planned military sites were targeted — a number higher than the 323-drone intercept count would normally allow if each drone hit a single target. The arithmetic: 323 drones for 48 targets averages 6.7 drones per target, suggesting both saturation strikes and pre-identified target lists.

Fourth, Zelensky's HUR briefing on air-defense redeployment is the structural admission that coverage has been degraded. Zelensky said on 24 June, citing military intelligence (HUR), that Ukraine's long-range strike campaign has forced Russia to redeploy air defense systems to protect Moscow and the Kerch Bridge, weakening coverage in other Russian regions and occupied territories. This is the structural admission that air defense coverage has been degraded — incompatible with the 323-interception claim of denial. The Russian MoD's regional list is the operational consequence: when air defenses are concentrated on Moscow and the Kerch Bridge, the 17 other named regions are where the strikes land.

Fifth, the continuity layer. The 21 June gas-sales suspension in occupied Crimea predates this overnight strike by three days — indicating that the 24-25 June strikes are part of a cumulative pattern of degradation, not a single isolated incident. Half of Crimea was without electricity after the overnight strikes. Russian-occupation authorities were already managing a fuel crisis; the overnight strikes have now added a sustained power outage on top of it. The operational pattern — strikes on energy + fuel infrastructure designed to force Russian-occupation authorities into emergency-procedure mode — is the same pattern the 20-21 June Crimea Bridge corridor strike set up, but scaled up to 19 regions and the largest occupied-Crimean city.

Sixth, the Orenburg continuity. The Orenburg gas-processing plant strike was covered in the prior 24 June article. The Carpet air restriction regime was introduced at Orenburg airports after the strike, with Orenburg, Orsk, and Yasny temporarily suspending operations. The Orenburg strike is the third deep-strike archetype in the Russia/Ukraine beat (after Tyumen 1,900 km on 20 June and Krasnodar Poltavskaya depot/pumping layer earlier). The 24-25 June overnight strike is the cumulative denial-vs-physical-evidence article — it does not focus on any single strike site but on the structural contradiction between the MoD's count and the regional impact.

Beat-distinct from the Orenburg article of 24 June, the VZPP-S Voronezh article of 22 June, the Crimea Bridge corridor strike of 20-21 June, and all prior Russia/Ukraine pieces. The denial-side is the Russian MoD's 323-interception count; the physical-evidence side is the cumulative 19-region impact plus the Sevastopol substation, the Saky hangars, the S-400/Pantsir losses near Kerch, and the gas-sales continuity since 21 June.
verdict: On the night of 24-25 June 2026, the Russian MoD claimed it intercepted 323 Ukrainian drones overnight — but the same MoD statement lists 19 Russian regions, the Sea of Azov, and the Black Sea as affected. The MoD's own geography contradicts its own count: a 'near-total interception' that hits 19 federal subjects, a sea, and a peninsula is operationally incoherent. Razvozhayev's Telegram admission — 'We will not be intimidated by the lack of light' — is the first on-record acknowledgement from a Russian-installed official that a Ukrainian strike knocked out power in Sevastopol, the largest occupied-Crimean city. The 'special regime' formulation at energy facilities is the same emergency-procedure language used after prior major Crimean strikes, confirming this is a confirmed hit, not a near-miss. The SBU confirmed damage to four aircraft storage hangars at Saky and to two S-400 components and two Pantsir-S1 systems near Kerch — high-value strategic assets incompatible with the 323-interception framing. Zelensky's HUR briefing on Russian air-defense redeployment to Moscow and the Kerch Bridge is the structural admission that coverage has been degraded. Beat-distinct from the Orenburg article of 24 June (gas-plant thermal hotspots, single site) and from all prior Russia/Ukraine pieces — this is the cumulative denial-vs-physical-evidence article covering the 19-region overnight strike.
